classification.difficultyReason: Find an integer root, reduce the cubic, and choose factorisation or the quadratic formula while checking whether additional real roots exist.

answer.worked:
Let $P(x)=x^3+x^2-4x+2$.
$$\begin{align*}P(1)&=1+1-4+2\\P(1)&=0.\end{align*}$$
Hence $x-1$ is a factor. Long division gives
$$P(x)=(x-1)(x^2+2x-2).$$
By the zero-product rule, $x=1$ or $x^2+2x-2=0$. For the quadratic,
$$\begin{align*}x&=\frac{-2\pm\sqrt{2^2-4(1)(-2)}}{2}\\x&=\frac{-2\pm\sqrt{12}}{2}\\x&=-1\pm\sqrt3.\end{align*}$$
Therefore $x=1,\ -1+\sqrt3,\ -1-\sqrt3$.

Let $P(x)=x^3+8x^2+21x+18$.
$$\begin{align*}P(-2)&=-8+32-42+18\\P(-2)&=0.\end{align*}$$
Hence $x+2$ is a factor. Long division and quadratic factorisation give
$$\begin{align*}P(x)&=(x+2)(x^2+6x+9)\\P(x)&=(x+2)(x+3)^2.\end{align*}$$
By the zero-product rule, $x=-2$ or $x=-3$.

Let $P(x)=x^3-4x^2+7x-6$.
$$\begin{align*}P(2)&=8-16+14-6\\P(2)&=0.\end{align*}$$
Hence $x-2$ is a factor. Long division gives
$$P(x)=(x-2)(x^2-2x+3).$$
For $x^2-2x+3=0$,
$$\begin{align*}\Delta&=(-2)^2-4(1)(3)\\\Delta&=-8.\end{align*}$$
The quadratic has no real roots, so the only real solution is $x=2$.

Let $P(x)=x^3-15x+4$.
$$\begin{align*}P(-4)&=-64+60+4\\P(-4)&=0.\end{align*}$$
Hence $x+4$ is a factor. Long division gives
$$P(x)=(x+4)(x^2-4x+1).$$
By the zero-product rule, $x=-4$ or $x^2-4x+1=0$. For the quadratic,
$$\begin{align*}x&=\frac{4\pm\sqrt{(-4)^2-4(1)(1)}}{2}\\x&=\frac{4\pm\sqrt{12}}{2}\\x&=2\pm\sqrt3.\end{align*}$$
Therefore $x=-4,\ 2+\sqrt3,\ 2-\sqrt3$.
